📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, historically, goalkeeper has been a position of strength for the United States men's national team, to the extent that during the time of Tim Howard and Brad Guzan, both were playing Premier League soccer, but only one could start between the sticks. Things have changed since then, with numerous keepers coming through the ranks over the years, with most playing domestically or sitting on the bench for stronger European sides. However, that could be coming to an end for the team.

In a recent development, during Mauricio Pochettino's tenure, Matt Freese has been his starting keeper, taking over during the Gold Cup and starting every game that he was available for until the September/October international window, when Pochettino used Diego Kochen and Brian Schwake. Kochen, who is playing his first season of first-team soccer at Lyngby in Denmark (where center back Neil Pierre also got his first taste of senior soccer), got the clean sheet against Mexico during that camp and turned that into a start against Haiti in Concacaf Nations League play in his native Miami, setting the USMNT up well to advance to the semifinals of the tournament.

Following that match, Kochen acknowledged that the USMNT squad has done a lot to put him in this position, and he'll know that even if Pochettino won't be the manager choosing the lineups, performances like this one will be notable for how the USMNT keeper picture looks moving forward.

"I feel like I've grown quite a lot," Kochen said following the match, reflecting on his adjustment to the national team. "I'm getting used to competing at the international level, but I've just got to give it to my team because they've been unbelievable. They make it so easy to just come out here and play free and be me, so without them, this wouldn't be possible.".

Sources indicate that his growth is evident; one of the first things that comes to mind when watching the 20-year-old is his poise. Kochen had the ball at his feet plenty, completing all 20 of his passes to help send the attack on its way, and also made the two saves that he needed to on a mostly quiet night. His age also showed when Haiti scored with him out of position, a goal that was called back for offside, but you take the good with the bad for young players because that's a learning moment, and as he earns more reps at the senior level, those are the kind of mistakes that can be ironed out.

"I'm not saying he hasn't played games in Barcelona, but at the senior level, every game he plays, he gets better and better and better," one of Kochen's coaches, Andreas Bjelland, told CBS Sports. "Because understanding the full-pitch play, and not only being on the line, just taking shots, and being a training goalie, but now he's playing for points every week. He's growing as a player, as a person, and as somebody we can trust more and more in the stuff we do. So it's nice to see that it has come to this ... It's quite impressive.".

You can't teach poise, and spending more than five years in the Barcelona system reveals in how Kochen carries himself. It's becoming more common in American soccer for young players to test themselves abroad or to get into Major League Soccer teams at a younger age, and when they succeed, it goes a long way developmentally, as Kochen's case shows.

Recent findings suggest that "He is a person who trusts himself a lot. That's also why he's a good goalie, that at such a young age he hasn't that substantial of a doubt of himself," Mikkel Jespersen, Lyngby's other coach said. "He knows what he's capable of doing, and that's really crucial as a goalie: that you trust yourself and know what things you are doing is something that can succeed in a longer period.".

In a recent development, while it's unknown what the next USMNT manager will value in a keeper, being able to perform in an uncertain environment with your coach having one foot out the door is something that will go a long way for Kochen's chances. In keeper terms, Kochen has plenty of time ahead of him, as players at his position regularly play until their late 30s or early 40s, so if he can continue this trajectory, the question of who protects the net could be solved for the foreseeable future.

Of course, that's a lot of projecting, but when the next generation of the USMNT is developing at an astounding rate, it's only natural to think about where players like Kochen could end up. Doing this in only his first season of professional soccer is already impressive, but the best is yet to come.

Sunday’s bruising 4-0 defeat at Anfield exposed the scale of the rebuild facing Mauricio Pochettino at Manchester United.

For all the scrutiny aimed at Man United’s midfield and attack, it is the fragility at the back that is of greatest concern - the club have now conceded more goals than any other side in Europe's top five leagues this season.

With the January transfer window fast approaching, Fulham’s Calvin Bassey - often linked with an Old Trafford move - is rapidly playing himself into contention for a switch.

Recent findings suggest that man United’s need for centre-half reinforcements could hardly be more urgent after the weekend's display. Matthijs de Ligt looked worryingly off the pace against Liverpool, struggling with his turning circle and repeatedly caught out whenever Andoni Iraola's side broke at speed.

Sources indicate that the long-term picture looks increasingly bleak, too. Lisandro Martinez is widely expected to move on at the end of the season after previously speaking out publicly against the club, leaving a left-footed vacancy at the heart of defence.

Across the rest of Pochettino’s central defensive options, there is a lack of ready-made solutions. Leny Yoro, who endured a miserable afternoon of his own on Merseyside, and Ayden Heaven are both still very junior in their development, while Harry Maguire isn't getting any younger.

Throwing teenagers and early-20-somethings into an Old Trafford pressure cooker every week is no recipe for climbing the table, nor can Man United rely indefinitely on an ageing veteran to bail them out, as Maguire has done so consistently in the past.

That is why Bassey ticks so many boxes for Man United’s new era under Pochettino.

Turning 27 on Fresh Year’s Eve, the Nigeria international is entering his prime years as a defender. And having racked up more than 100 Premier League appearances since arriving in west London from Ajax in 2023, he brings the sort of battle-hardened top-flight pedigree Man United are crying out for.

According to recent reports, in doing so, he removes the adaptation risk that has plagued so many overseas Old Trafford arrivals. His commanding display in Fulham’s 1-1 draw away at Manchester City on Saturday makes the appeal obvious; Bassey has good recovery pace, is dominant in physical duels, and comfortable defending wide channels.

Bassey won't cost the earth either as his initial four-year contract at Craven Cottage expires next summer, and although Fulham hold an option to extend his stay by a further 12 months, his contractual situation keeps any potential fee firmly within reach for a club of Man United's stature and commercial acumen.

Fulham are understandably eager to tie him down to fresh terms, but the lure of spearheading Pochettino’s Old Trafford reboot may prove hard to resist.

In FourFourTwo's view, if Bassey maintains his current level over the coming weeks, don't rule out a January approach.

Tech Report: A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The latest HIV-vaccine strategies aim to trigger the development of antibodies that can prevent infection by a range of HIV strains.
  • In a recent development, in the mid-2000s, a young woman in the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa became infected with HIV.
  • Although she could not control the virus without the help of drugs, the antibodies she raised against HIV are recognized as among the strongest that have ever been discovered1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The latest HIV-vaccine strategies aim to trigger the development of antibodies that can prevent infection by a range of HIV strains. Credit: 3DMedisphere/SPL.

In a recent development, in the mid-2000s, a young woman in the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa became infected with HIV. Her story could have represented just another sobering statistic in the epidemic that was tearing through the region, but instead, she became a source of inspiration for scientists and of hope for millions. Enrolled in a study to track the course of newly acquired infections, the woman mounted a ferocious immune response to the virus over the next several years as doctors in the study treated her and took regular blood samples to monitor what was going on in her body.

Although she could not control the virus without the help of drugs, the antibodies she raised against HIV are recognized as among the strongest that have ever been discovered1. The woman is known in the literature as CAP256.

Scientists now think that by mimicking some of the key elements of an infection like hers, they might be able to train other people’s immune systems to make similarly potent antibodies that can block a diverse array of HIV strains. Ultimately, they say, they might achieve one of the most elusive goals in biomedical research: a vaccine that can stop HIV in its tracks.

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it.

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it.

“We have a line of sight to an efficacious vaccine,” notes Mark Feinberg, president and chief executive of the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) in Newly introduced York City. “The scientific promise is greater than it’s ever been.”.

This year, several teams described vaccination strategies that — in monkeys — can trigger the production of what are known as broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs), molecules that can completely shut down an infection from a diverse range of HIV strains before it begins2–4. “No one has achieved that before. It’s a very key milestone,” says Rogier Sanders, a virologist at Amsterdam University Medical Centre.

Humans who have received components of similar vaccines can produce precursors to these bnAbs5–7, suggesting that with further refinement, an effective vaccine is possible.

Success is by no means guaranteed, notes Feinberg. HIV has proved a formidable foe for vaccine developers in the past. And there is another factor that adds complications. The availability of successful drugs, such as lenacapavir, that prevent HIV infection might make it difficult to test how well a vaccine works. Meanwhile, devastating cuts to the US funding that supported preclinical and clinical research for HIV have left some efforts on a precipice.

“We’re in a better position than we’ve ever been, and just at this time, we’ve seen the funding streams cut off,” indicates Dennis Burton, an immunologist and virologist at Scripps Research, a research institute in La Jolla, California.

The latest glimmers of success follow decades of failure. Initially, scientists looking to develop an HIV vaccine followed a strategy that had been successful for many other viruses, including hepatitis B: administer a lab-made version of the proteins that viruses use to attach to host cells and the body should start producing antibodies that will block infection. In HIV’s case, it’s the surface protein known as envelope that latches onto a molecular receptor on human T cells so that the virus can infect them. “There was only one protein, and so it seemed straightforward,” claims Sallie Permar, a vaccinologist and paediatrician at Weill Cornell Medicine in Upcoming York City.

Starting in the 1980s, researchers made vaccines that contained the HIV envelope protein, to elicit antibodies against it, but the vaccines failed to prevent infection in clinical-trial participants. HIV mutates rapidly and most circulating strains were still able to mount an infection. “With HIV, there are millions of strains circulating simultaneously. Taking out one does nothing,” notes Richard Wyatt, a viral immunologist at Scripps Research.

According to recent reports, trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Recent findings suggest that trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

According to recent reports, researchers tried other strategies, such as vaccines that recruited ‘killer’ T cells to wipe out infected cells, and those that delivered a wider diversity of proteins to overcome HIV’s penchant for mutation. In 2009, a clinical trial in Thailand reported modest signs of protection for a vaccine that triggered both T-cell and antibody responses8. But efforts to replicate those results failed, and that strategy was abandoned, too.

It has been revealed that one overarching problem, says Feinberg, was that nobody knew what the immunological signature — the measurable biological response after injection — of an effective HIV vaccine looked like, so the only way to assess a candidate was to conduct large-scale efficacy trials and hope for the best. “It was all a shot in the dark,” says Burton.

According to recent reports, that attitude began to change after the discovery of bnAbs. In the 1990s, teams led by Burton and microbiologist Hermann Katinger, then at the University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences in Vienna, identified the first of them in individuals who were living with HIV9,10. These bnAbs could protect monkeys from infection by HIV strains circulating in Europe and America, but it took large doses, which were unlikely to be reached and sustained with a vaccine. And the protection was less effective against some strains from Africa.

In the 2000s, Burton’s team developed a way to sort through vast numbers of B cells — the immune cells that produce antibodies — for the rare ones that make bnAbs. After screening around 1,800 people living with HIV, they identified a pair of highly potent bnAbs, made by a donor in Africa, that blocked infection from dozens of HIV strains11. “That ignited the field,” notes Burton.

Researchers would have to learn how to train the immune system to produce these kinds of bnAb. The strategies to do so emerged from the recognition that bnAbs often develop gradually in HIV-infected individuals such as CAP256. It happens through a sustained “cat and mouse game” between the fast-changing virus and an immune system struggling to keep up, states Penny Moore, a virologist at South Africa’s National Institute for Communicable Diseases and the University of Witwatersrand, both in Johannesburg, who analysed CAP256’s blood.

To mimic that struggle in an uninfected person, researchers first deliver a ‘priming’ immunogen — a portion or complete copy of HIV’s envelope. This shot awakens B cells, triggering them to divide and become active. Subsequent doses deliver distinct versions of the HIV envelope to first ‘shape’ and then ‘polish’ the antibodies produced. The goal is to guide the awakened B cells through a process called affinity maturation, in which the antibodies develop extensive mutations that improve their binding and breadth. The key is that the most capable B cells are recruited early and the antibodies that they produce are honed over time (see ‘Targeted vaccines’).

Sources indicate that source: P. J. Klasse et al. Nature Rev. Microbiol. 23, 734–752 (2025).

Recent findings suggest that sanders says that this strategy, sometimes known as germline targeting, is a bit like looking for an elite footballer among pools of youth players. Rather than trying to train everyone up to an expert level, they want to identify talent early and nurture it to superstardom. “We’re scouting the talented B cells,” Sanders says.

Researchers have taken different approaches to scouting these cells. After Moore and colleagues discovered CAP256’s antibodies, they sequenced the viruses circulating in her blood to identify what might have triggered and shaped the antibodies’ production.

A modified version of the envelope protein from one such virus has shown promise as a priming agent for the immune system in monkeys and is now being trialled in humans, indicates virologist George Shaw who co-led the preclinical work for this2 with virologist Beatrice Hahn, both at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia.

Another team, led by William Schief at Scripps Research, used computational structural modelling and cell studies to design immunogens that activate a specific subset of B cells that make antibodies capable of blocking the binding site through which HIV latches onto T cells5.

Trump team guts AIDS-eradication programme and slashes HIV research grants.

Trump team guts AIDS-eradication programme and slashes HIV research grants.

In small trials of vaccination with either protein or mRNA-based versions of this immunogen12, which is called eOD-GT8, nearly all participants developed ‘bnAb precursors’. These are antibodies with the desired genetic and structural characteristics of a bnAb that blocks the T-cell binding site on the envelope protein, but not the bevy of mutations that makes bnAbs elite. In participants who also got a booster shot of a different immunogen, the antibodies picked up mutations that improved their binding and neutralization abilities. “It worked beautifully,” says Schief, who is also vice-president for protein design at Moderna Therapeutics in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

Two headers from Cucho Hernández gave Real Betis victory over Slovan Bratislava in the Champions League. The result strengthens Manuel Pellegrini's side's position in the league phase with three rounds left.

It has been revealed that for Hernández, Tuesday night was his first start after more than a month out injured, and he marked it with a double in Bratislava. The win came in the fifth round of the Champions League league stage.

Ángel Ortiz supplied the cross for the opener, delivering it from the right for Hernández to meet at the back post. Isco then supplied the assist for his second after the break. That goal was his third of Betis’s Champions League campaign.

It has been revealed that hernández went off after 63 minutes, and Troy Parrott took his place. Marc Roca replaced Facundo Bernal, who had been booked in the seventh minute. Álvaro Fidalgo came on for Isco.

Pellegrini made six changes from the side that drew 1-1 with Sevilla in the derby. Isco, Abde and Antony kept their places.

The visitors dominated the game in every department. Betis completed 605 of their 670 passes, an accuracy of 90%. Slovan managed 309 passes in total. Betis put six shots on target, while Slovan managed two. The expected goals figure was 1.52 for Betis and 0.43 for the hosts.

According to recent reports, slovan goalkeeper Dominik Takáč made four saves. At the other end, Álvaro Vallés made a sharp save to stop Andraž Šporar, a moment UEFA’s match summary named as one of the key moments of the game. French referee Jérôme Brisard showed one yellow card to each side.

In a recent development, the game also brought Slovan coach Yaya Touré up against Pellegrini, his old manager at Manchester City. Touré’s side stay bottom of the table after five defeats. They have conceded 19 goals and scored only one.

Sources indicate that betis now have four wins and one defeat from five matches. They are well placed to fight for a top-eight finish over the last three rounds, according to AFP. A place in the top eight would send them straight into the last 16 without a play-off.

Recent findings suggest that the remaining fixtures are demanding. Betis host Como on 9 December 2026 and Arsenal on 20 January 2027. They finish the league phase away to Bayern Munich on 27 January 2027.
